big_idea: A BAR GRAPH uses bars instead of pictures. The bar HEIGHT shows the count.
learning_intention: We are learning to build bar graphs.
student_learning_goal: I can build a bar graph with title and labels.
success_criteria: I can draw a bar with the right HEIGHT.
I can write a TITLE and LABEL the axes.
I can read a bar graph.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot: A pictograph uses pictures. A BAR GRAPH uses bars! Each bar's HEIGHT is the count! Dot opens: 'Bar height equals…' Class: 'the COUNT!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot and Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday two-way tallies. Today BAR GRAPHS.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write BAR GRAPH on chart. 'Bar graph = a graph with bars. Bar height = count.'

Demo. Use yesterday's tally data: Snacks — apple 5, cookie 3, sandwich 4.

Draw a grid:
Y-axis: 0-6 (counts)
X-axis: apple, cookie, sandwich

Draw bars: apple bar reaches 5; cookie bar reaches 3; sandwich bar reaches 4.

Add: Title 'Favourite Snack'. Y-axis label 'Number of children'. X-axis label 'Snack'.

'Detective Dot says — every bar graph needs: TITLE, LABELS on both axes, and BARS the right HEIGHT.'

More examples:
- Sport: hockey 8, soccer 5, baseball 4. Bars 8, 5, 4.
- Pet: dog 6, cat 4, fish 2. Bars 6, 4, 2.

'Today we BUILD bar graphs from tally data.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: build a 4-category bar graph from class snack data.
Three stations. A: From Tally to Bar — convert a 4-category tally. B: Read a Bar Graph — answer 4 questions. C: Build Your Own — survey 6 classmates and graph.

steps.teacher_prompt: Show: bar graph without labels = unreadable.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their bar graphs for the same two-way table. Class compares: 'Same data, same heights? What if rows and columns were swapped — does the GRAPH change?' Cite Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001) levels — comparing two graphs of the same data is reading-between-the-data.
steps.teacher_prompt: Dot: 'Same counts, same heights. Different ORDER, same INFORMATION.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use pre-labeled grid.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children form 'living bar graph' lines by their answers.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: bar height matches count; writes title; labels axes.

discussion_prompts: What do AXIS LABELS tell us?
consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's bar-graph refrain — Dot calls 'Bar height equals…' Class: 'the COUNT!' Repeat 3x. Then 'Title, labels, axes — case CLEAR!' Each child reads one bar's count aloud.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child draws bars at WRONG HEIGHT — repairing the height-mismatch trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On bar graphs, the dominant Grade-2 trap is reading-the-data literally: child names the tallest bar without articulating that bar HEIGHT corresponds to a COUNT. Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001, 'Making Sense of Graphs', JRME) frame graph comprehension as reading-the-data → reading-between-the-data → reading-beyond-the-data; G2 children operate at level 1 and need explicit scaffolding to articulate height-as-count.

Yesterday Lesson 2's two-way table holds the data. Today we DISPLAY it as a bar graph. Lesson 4 finds mode; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Tally shows apple = 3. Child draws apple bar to height 5 on the grid.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You drew apple to 5. But the tally says 3. Detective Dot asks — what should the height be?'

Guide. Count tally marks. 'Three. So bar should reach 3 on the y-axis.' Erase, redraw to 3.

Generalise. 'Bar height EQUALS the count. Every count check before drawing.'

If still mismatching: provide a 'count-check' before drawing each bar. 'Look at the y-axis number. Match.'

Long-term recovery: every bar starts with 'count-check'.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Reads bar graph back to verify.
common_misconceptions: Tallest bar = mode. (Repair: yes, but at G2 we say 'most popular'.)
Bars can be any width. (Repair: same width, varying height.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names tallest bar without counting: drill 'bar height = COUNT'; child counts grid units up the bar before naming.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child reads height incorrectly (off-by-one): use a numbered grid background; child reads the topmost grid number the bar reaches.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child cannot connect bar to category: highlight the x-axis label; child says 'THIS bar (pointing) shows COUNT of THIS category (axis label).'

parts_outline.task: Read a bar graph. Answer 4 questions.
Build a bar graph from tally data (4 categories).
Survey 5 classmates. Build your own bar graph.
